title: Virtual school vs. homeschool: key differences and how to decide
summary: Public virtual school, private online school, and homeschooling compared: curriculum control, cost, flexibility, and how to decide which fits your family.
body_markdown:
## How homeschooling works


Homeschooling puts you in the driver's seat. You pick the curriculum, or build your own, or skip formal curriculum entirely. You set the daily schedule. You decide whether your kid studies history through a textbook, a documentary series, or a visit to a battlefield.


Some homeschool families follow a structured daily plan that mirrors a school day. Others take an interest-led approach that follows a kid's curiosity.[Unschooling](https://outschool.com/articles/unschooling) , at one end of the spectrum, removes formal curriculum almost entirely. Most families land somewhere in the middle.


Homeschooling isn't free, but it doesn't have to be expensive. Families spend anywhere from a few hundred dollars using library resources and free materials to several thousand a year on curriculum, classes, and enrichment. In a growing number of states,[education savings accounts (ESAs)](https://outschool.com/esa-guides/what-is-education-savings-account) cover many of those costs.


Where homeschooling gets most interesting is the support network you build.[Co-ops](https://outschool.com/homeschool/what-is-homeschool-co-op) , live online classes, tutors, and community programs let you hand off the subjects you're less confident teaching while you keep control of the overall plan.


**Best for:** Families who want maximum flexibility and customization, are comfortable directing their kid's education with or without outside support, and want to tailor learning to their kid's pace, interests, and needs.


## The key differences compared


### Who controls the curriculum?


Public virtual school: the program. Private online school: the school, though you chose it for its specific approach. Homeschool: you.


### Schedule flexibility


Public virtual school: minimal, with required attendance windows and deadlines. Private online school: moderate, and it varies by program. Homeschool: complete flexibility.


### Teacher involvement


Public virtual school: an assigned state-certified teacher. Private online school: school-employed teachers, often with smaller classes. Homeschool: you are the teacher, supplemented with whatever outside support you choose.


### Cost


Public virtual school: free. Private online school: tuition, which varies widely by school. Homeschool: from very little to several thousand dollars a year, sometimes offset by ESA funds.


### Records and transcripts


Public virtual school: official district transcripts and diploma. Private online school: the school issues transcripts and a diploma. Homeschool: parent-generated transcripts and portfolio, and some families use an umbrella school for extra credentialing.


### Social opportunities


Public virtual school: limited, and it varies by program. Private online school: built in through cohorts, clubs, and virtual events. Homeschool: organized by parents through co-ops, community activities, and online class communities.


## How to decide


Start with three questions.


**How much control do you want?** If you want to design every aspect of your kid's education, homeschooling is the clear fit. If you'd rather someone else handle the curriculum and teaching while you supervise, virtual school, public or private, makes more sense.


**What's your budget?** Public virtual school is free. Homeschooling can be inexpensive. Private online school usually costs the most. If cost is a factor,[check whether your state offers an ESA](https://outschool.com/esa-guides/what-is-education-savings-account) that could offset private school or homeschool expenses.


**What does your kid need right now?** A kid who thrives on structure and peer interaction might do well in a private online school with cohort-based learning. A kid who needs to move at their own pace, or whose interests don't fit a standard curriculum, is often better served by homeschooling. A kid who needs to leave their current school for a free alternative may be well served by public virtual school.


You can also mix models. Plenty of homeschool families enroll a kid in a single virtual school course, like lab science or a foreign language, while homeschooling everything else. And many families who start with one model switch after a year or two as their kid's needs change.


## Where Outschool fits


Outschool isn't a virtual school or a curriculum. It's a marketplace of live online classes taught by independent teachers, covering everything from algebra to creative writing. Families across all three models use it differently.


Homeschoolers use it as their main class source or to fill gaps in subjects they don't want to teach themselves. Private online school families add electives and enrichment their school doesn't offer. Public virtual school families add small-group classes that give more interaction and depth than their program allows.


If you're exploring your options,[browse Outschool's classes for homeschool families](https://outschool.com/online-classes/homeschooling) .


## Frequently asked questions


### Is virtual school the same as homeschool?


No. In virtual school, public or private, your kid is enrolled in a school with assigned teachers and a set curriculum. In homeschooling, you direct the education yourself under your state's homeschool law. Some states also report and classify the two differently.


### Can I switch from virtual school to homeschool mid-year?


In most states, yes, but the paperwork depends on where you live. Florida requires a written notice of intent to the district superintendent within 30 days of starting a home education program \[1\]. New York requires a letter of intent within 14 days of beginning home instruction \[4\]. Withdraw from the virtual program first, file what your state requires, and request your kid's records. Our guide to[switching from traditional school to homeschooling](https://outschool.com/homeschool/switching-from-traditional-school-to-homeschooling) covers the first 90 days, including a December or January switch.


### Are private online schools accredited?


Many are, but accreditation varies. Ask the school which agency accredits it, confirm directly with that agency, and check with the colleges your kid may apply to.


### Can I use ESA funds for private online school tuition?


It depends on the program. Louisiana's LA GATOR program lists tuition and fees at a participating nonpublic school or for nonpublic online learning programs as an approved expense \[5\]. In Texas, online programs qualify if the provider applies and is accepted into the program \[6\]. Read your state's approved expense list, and see our guide to[what ESA funds cover](https://outschool.com/esa-guides/approved-list) .
